Al-qiṭṭ is said to be the written deed (ṣakk) for a gift (jāʾiza).
Al-Aʿshā uses the plural, quṭūṭ, in a line on King al-Nuʿmān "giving out the quṭūṭ" on the day the poet met him.
those who said it meant, as it were, the documents of reward they are given in the Hereafter
one family built on the number "four" and its derivatives
أربعة (four), أربعون (forty), رُبع (a quarter), رُباع (four at a time)
a single root whose core idea is throwing, pelting, or flinging
الرَّدَى is destruction; رَدِيَ يَرْدَى = "he perished"; أَرْدَاهُ اللَّهُ = "God destroyed him."
التَّرَدِّي is plunging into a chasm
one single, regular meaning: assisting and backing someone by giving — a gift or other support
الرَّفْد (al-rafd) is the verbal noun of "rafadahu" — he gave him [something]
"Urfidtu al-māl" — I was given/granted the wealth
Ibn Fāris cites a line of al-Farazdaq mentioning "Iraq and its two Rāfids."
A ḥadīth uses it: "the fayʾ [war-gained wealth] becomes rifd"
one central image — the leg/foot (rijl) of any creature that has one
الرِّجْل (al-rijl) — the leg/foot of a human or animal
foot-soldiers/infantry (al-rajjāla), so named because they travel on their feet
الرَّجُل (al-rajul) — a "man," a single adult male
Cited verse: a vow to visit "the House of God, on foot and barefoot."
**flinging or casting a thing away**
رَمَيْتُ الشَّيْءَ أَرْمِيهِ — "I threw (or shot at) the thing, I throw it."
"going in search of something" — a compound notion combining *going* and *seeking*.
Al-sa'āma is weariness/tedium that comes from something continuing too long
Supporting verse of poetry: "I have grown weary of life's burdens; whoever lives eighty years grows weary"
the succession of many things, each connected to the next
glossed as ensuring the proportion between rivet and hole is exact, neither too tight nor too loose
al-sard — a collective term for chainmail and similar ring-linked work
وَرى (with fatḥa; also the dialectal wariya with kasra) = to produce/give out fire
وارَيْتُ الشيءَ = I hid the thing; تَوارى = he hid himself
وَراءَ (warāʾ) = "behind," but can also mean "in front / ahead,"
Al-Jawharī reads the Qurʾānic "and behind them was a king" (18:79) as meaning "ahead of them."
a single governing sense, which he takes from al-Khalīl: **concealing something**
خَدَعْتُ الرجل — "I deceived the man," glossed as ختلته (I tricked / caught him off guard)
Cited proverb: «الحرب خُدَعة» ("war is trickery")
"to increase, grow, add, exceed"
Of a thing growing of itself: زاد ("increased") — of water or wealth
Of causing growth: God "increased him in wealth"
Of exceeding: "he exceeded what he intended"
Cited from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī: "you are a company exceeding a hundred; so gather your whole affair and scheme against me"
the governing sense (taʾwīl) of baʿth as the removal of whatever was holding something back from acting or moving
highlights.note: Ibn Sīda's governing sense of baʿth

highlights.text: To send. بَعَثَهُ (baʿathahu) = to send someone on his own
بَعَثَ اللهُ الخلق, which Ibn Sīda glosses as nasharahum
highlights.note: God raising creation, as in the Qur'an

highlights.text: illustrated by a line of Ḥumayd b. Thawr on a careworn man kept sleepless by his worries
highlights.note: Ḥumayd b. Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: a single root whose core idea is one thing encircling or surrounding another from its sides
**دَارَتْ بِهِمُ الدَّوَائِر** — "adverse turns of fortune encircled them," i.e., disliked conditions surrounded them.
The base verb is دَارَ / يَدُورُ (to turn, revolve), verbal noun دَوَرَان.
Cited: "and time, with man, is ever-turning."
Ibn Fāris cites two prophetic ḥadīths using dūr/dār for tribes
a single sound root whose core notion is a thing flowing or running easily
فَاضَ الْمَاءُ (fāḍa al-māʾ), "the water overflowed."
أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ مِنْ عَرَفَةَ, "the people poured forth from ʿArafa," i.e. they pushed off in a body
أَفَاضَ الْقَوْمُ فِي الْحَدِيثِ, "they launched into the conversation," i.e. threw themselves into it
أَعْطَاهُ غَيْضًا مِنْ فَيْضٍ, "he gave him a ghayḍ out of a fayḍ," glossed as "a little out of much."
The core idea running through the whole entry is covering / enveloping (taghṭiya).
(yughshī al-layl al-nahār) "He covers the night with the day"
ghashiyahu al-amr / taghashshāhu = the affair enveloped him
All mean "a covering" (ghiṭāʾ).
Ibn Sīda cites Jaʿfar ibn ʿUlba al-Ḥārithī: "We share our swords with them in the worst division: ours the coverings, theirs the edges."
the al-ghāshiya is glossed either as the Resurrection (it envelops all creation) or as the Fire (it envelops the faces of the deniers)
a single sound root whose core notion is one thing gripping or clinging to another with force
الكَلْب (al-kalb), the familiar animal
الكَلَّاب (al-kallāb) and المُكَلِّب (al-mukallib) are terms for the man who trains a dog to hunt
"we paid for our slain with the like of them, and with uncounted shackled captives"
Ibn Fāris identifies one core meaning for this root, with two intertwined strands: gathering/collecting, and nearness/closeness.
Kathīb (كَثِيب), "sand dune" — a heap of sand, again from the idea of things gathered together.
A line of poetry by al-Nābighah is cited, describing spears displayed "above the kawāthib" (i.e., held up over the horses' withers).
a single sound root whose core idea is passing one thing over another with a flat, spreading motion — wiping, stroking, smoothing
to pass the hand (or something) flat over a surface — "I wiped/stroked it with my hand" (masaḥtuhu bi-yadī, verbal noun masḥ)
whose single unifying idea is taraddud — repeated back-and-forth motion, surging or wavering movement
a she-camel "tamūru" (sways/surges) as she moves, and is called "mawwāra," swift
"Al-mawr" as wave — the surging swell of water.
Ṭarafa's ode is quoted describing such a camel
Striking / hollowing out / decay
Scooping / ladling
Qadaḥa, in its basic sense, means to strike or gouge into something
The verb also covers striking fire (qadaḥtu l-nār)
measuring or estimating one thing against another
Al-qaws = the dhira', a forearm-length unit of measurement — named this because it is the standard by which something is measured. The same word names the qaws, the archer's bow.
Cited: a verse of Imru' al-Qays on women not loving a poor or grey-haired, stooped man.
the exegetes gloss this as "two forearm-lengths."
taking something swiftly and by snatching it away
Basic sense — stripping/snatching: salabtuhu thawbahu ("I stripped/snatched his garment from him").
He quotes Labīd's line mentioning "the black sulub-garments... and the amsāḥ [coarse cloth]."
A hadith is cited: "Whoever kills a [combatant] in battle, the salab [the slain man's weapons and gear] belongs to him."
al-salwa — a bird identified with quail (al-suman)
Illustrated with a line of poetry by Ru'bah
Al-thayyib, applied to a woman, is one who married and then separated from her husband — by any means — after he had had intercourse with her.
God's words "thayyibātin wa-abkāran" (Q. 66:5) — "previously-married women and virgins"
"The two thayyibs are stoned; the two virgins (bikrs) are flogged and exiled"
a single root with one core idea: the falling / dropping of something
وَقَعَ الشَّيْءُ وُقُوعًا — "the thing fell/occurred"; the active participle is وَاقِعٌ ("falling, befalling")
الْوَاقِعَة — "that which befalls,"
"everything you gather and carry, you have wasaqtahu."
"The moon ittasaqa" — became full/complete, its light aligned into wholeness.
"wa'l-layli wa-mā wasaq" — "by the night, and what it wasaq [gathers/enshrouds]"
Labīd uses this in a verse describing a garden: on the day provision became abundant, the palms were mūsiqāt (heavily laden) and other growth was copious and first-yielding.
Core sense — the colour green.
الخُضْرة is the familiar colour.
The saying "Beware the greenery of the dung-heaps" is applied to a beautiful woman of bad origin
**snatching something away quickly and lightly**
الخَطْف = snatching away
بَرْقٌ خَاطِفٌ — lightning described as snatching away the light of the eyes.
The shayṭān "snatches" hearing, i.e. steals it furtively.
Cited from al-Nābigha: "crooked hooks on stout ropes, drawn toward you by hands pulling hard."
two base senses: (1) proportioning/measuring out a thing, and (2) smoothness of a thing
خُلُق (khuluq) = inborn disposition or temperament (السجية), so called because its possessor has been "proportioned"/determined upon it.
الخَلَاق (al-khalāq) = one's allotted share or portion, because each person's share has been apportioned to him.
Zuhayr's line contrasting one who "cuts out what he has measured"
some take the word as a reduplicated form belonging with the weak roots, from zāḥa, yazīḥu, "to draw back"
Others say it is taken from al-zawḥ, "hard driving", and likewise al-dhawḥ.
glossing zuḥziḥa as "moved aside and put at a distance"
zaḥḥahu and zaḥzaḥahu: he pushed him and moved him from his place, and put him at a distance from it
From zāḥa come Labīd's line "he drew back (zāḥa) from a stand like mine, and moved away"
"Whoever fasts a day in the way of God, God will move him (zaḥzaḥahu) seventy autumns away from the Fire"
zafara (yazfuru): to pant/groan with a heavy exhalation, like the groan of a mother who has lost a child (zafrat al-thaklā). The noun for this groaning sound is zafīr.
Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line is cited: an inherited glory "whose zawāfir have not failed it."
whose core notion is **putting at a distance, driving away**
طَرَدْتُهُ ṭaradtuhu — "I drove him away."
With the ruler as subject, forms IV and II (أَطْرَدَهُ / طَرَّدَهُ) mean to banish someone from his town
Do you recognise a trace, like the running-on of streaked patterns, belonging to ʿAmra — desolate, save for a rider's halting-place?
treats b-r-d as having four independent bases, with all derived forms tracing back to one of them
barada / bārid: to be cold, cold.
saḥāb barid: a cloud carrying hail (barad).
a verse promises a she-camel that "will cool livers and set mourners weeping."
evidenced by a verse on gazelles pillowed on the arṭā bush's "two cool sides."
treats d-n-w as nearness (al-dunūw = al-qurb), whether nearness in essence or nearness in status and judgement
The palm tree's "clusters hanging near" (qinwān dāniya, Q 6:99) show the plain sense.
**First**, against "last": al-dunyā against al-ākhira
adnā means it is nearer, for their own souls, to aiming at justice in testifying
In the saying "when you eat, fa-dannū", al-Rāghib derives the word from al-dūn ("what is near/below"), giving the sense "eat from what is next to you"
treats j-d-r as two independent roots
جِدَار (jidār) = a wall; plurals جُدُر (judur) and جُدْرَان (judrān)
هو جَدِيرٌ بكذا (huwa jadīrun bi-kadhā), "he is fit/worthy of it,"
derives every sense of the root ج-ل-س (j-l-s) from one core meaning: rising/elevation (al-irtifāʿ)
jalasa describes the transition from lying down or sleep into a sitting position
several lines of poetry (al-Hudhalī and others) using jalasa/al-jālis in this "went up to Najd" sense
turns on "coming into being / being brought forth" and, from that, "growing up."
"God brought creation forth (anshaʾa), so it came to be (nashaʾū)."
Qur'anic phrase "الجوار المنشآت" — the running ships with sails hoisted.
with the Qur'anic phrase "من ينشّؤا في الحلية" ("one reared amid ornament")
A verse of al-Shammākh uses mustanshaʾāt ("raised-up things") of howdah-like shapes
a single sound root whose core sense is: striking something until a dent or hollow is beaten into it
naqīr: the small speck on the back of a date-stone
He cites a woman's saying to her husband: take me past the men of naẓarā (who look) but not past the women of naqarā (who backbite)
God would not leave off from the slayer of a believer, i.e. not desist from punishing him
قَصَا – يَقْصُو – قُصُوّاً is to move away or stand apart, said of anything
القاصية (al-qāṣiya) describes both people and places that are remote and set apart
Ruʾba: "it leaves the soil of the deserts with its dust-clouds driven wild."
hanging something on something so that it stays attached to it
a share, a portion
taqlīd — putting a mark on the neck.
maqālīd — said to mean treasuries or storehouses
Ibn Fāris cites the poet Bishr: "Your patron bestowed it on you out of rancour — and Jaʿfar was collared with it as with a dove's ring-collar."
sets out three genuine base-meanings for this root
Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 22:21, "wa-lahum maqāmiʿu min ḥadīd" ("for them are maces of iron")
He quotes the pre-Islamic/early poet Aws (ibn Ḥajar): God sent down His help, while the dust-colored gazelles in their lairs go on warding off flies (taqammaʿu).
A ḥadīth calls certain people "the funnels of speech" (aqmāʿ al-qawl): those who hear but retain nothing, as if their ears were funnels that hold nothing back
whose single idea is: mingling with a thing, getting entangled in it, and putting it on like a garment
اقْتَرَفَ (iqtarafa) = to acquire or gain something
a people complained of the pestilence of their land and were told, "Move away, for from al-qaraf comes destruction."
two sound root meanings: cold, and firm establishment (settling in place)
Qarra and istaqarra: to settle, to become settled
may God give him enough that his eye rests and does not look longingly to anyone above him
Imruʾ al-Qays: "when they mount the horses and put on their mail, the earth burns, though the day is cold (qarr)."
a single consistent root meaning breadth/spaciousness and moving out freely across the land
سَرَب / سَرِب (sarab, sarib) — water leaking or flowing from a water-skin
سَارِب (sārib) — one going forth openly in the land
Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, "What ails your eye that water pours from it, as though it were a leak from the split seams of a water-skin"
sāḥa al-māʾ describes water flowing/streaming over the ground
sāḥa fī al-arḍ means to travel or roam through the land (siyāḥa)
Al-Zamakhshari cites the Qur'anic phrase "so travel/roam through the land" as the model usage
A verse attributed to Abu Talib is quoted about the sāʾiḥīn tasting no drop for their Lord's sake (the second half of the line is textually uncertain
to join/connect one thing to another (waṣala … fa-ttaṣala, "he joined it, and it became joined")
Form II waṣṣala (tawṣīl) = to splice or link repeatedly; cited with Qurʾān 28:51, "We have joined together the discourse for them."
a ewe that "accompanied"/was paired with her brother among the flock's young and so was spared slaughter
ittaṣala / waṣala ilā a tribe = to attach oneself, claim lineage (verse of al-Aʿshā)
khaṭṭa al-kitāb — to write a document
wa lā takhuṭṭuhu bi-yamīnika" — "nor did you write it with your right hand"
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah about an unmatched rival at the Battle of ʿUkāẓ
derives the whole root خ-ب-ط from one core idea: treading and striking
the verb يَتَخَبَّطُ here carries the same "being struck/buffeted" image
treats خ-ر-ق as a single root meaning to tear something open and to cut/pass through it
The poet Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī got his name from his line "upon it are the feathers and the rags."
An Arab saying: "She has neither a height that disparages her nor a shortness that abashes her"
al-yaqīn is knowledge that removes doubt and settles a matter as certain — the opposite of doubt, as knowledge is the opposite of ignorance
all meaning "to be/become certain of a matter"
al-yaqan = al-yaqīn, with a shāhid from al-Aʿshā
glossed as "until death comes to you," i.e. worship Him always, to the point of death
z-h-q as one root meaning: to move forward, to pass on, to go past a limit
زَهَقَتْ نَفْسُهُ — "his soul departed."
زَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ — falsehood zahaqa, glossed by him simply as "it passed away, went off."
Shāhid from Zuhayr, contrasting the mounts of a war-leader: "among them the lean and among them the fat, grease-laden (al-zāhiq al-zahim)."
derives ṭ-r-f from two distinct roots: (1) the edge or border of a thing, and (2) a movement of the eyelids
ṭaraf = the edge/tip of a thing, a garment, or a wall
originally the movement of the eyelids in looking; by extension it also names the eye itself
eyes with a languorous "sickness" in their glance slay their lovers yet do not revive them
Opposite of light.
Putting a thing out of its proper place, wrongfully.
The base word is ظُلْمَة (ẓulma, darkness; plural ظُلُمَات), also called ظَلَام (ẓalām)
The verb ظَلَمَ / يَظْلِمُ / ظُلْم means to wrong.
cited with Kaʿb's line ("...and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong")
highlights.note: proverb with Kaʿb, lived into Islam

highlights.text: illustrated by Zuhayr's line about a generous man "sometimes wronged, so he bears it" (fa-yaẓẓalimu)
treats b-q-y as a single root meaning permanence / enduring (al-dawām)
baqiyya / buqyā = sparing, clemency, mercy shown to someone
Shāhid from al-Nābigha: you will not "keep" a brother you never reproach for a fault, since no man is entirely faultless.
The ḥadīth of Muʿādh «بَقَيْنَا رسولَ الله» ("we waited for the Messenger of God") uses this "waiting" sense.
treats B–W–L as two separate roots: (1) fluid that seeps or flows out; (2) al-rūʿ — the inner part of a person into which a thought falls
مَا خَطَرَ بِبَالِي, "it never crossed my bāl," glossed as "it was not cast into my rūʿ (inward self)."
a wineskin that bursts and gushes its drink; attested in ʿAdī's poetry
Ibn Muqbil's verse uses the phrase for the mirage of the Ḥimyarī uplands
He cites Ibn ʿAbbās, asked about performing wuḍūʾ with milk: "I do not mind it in the least; be easy and you will be dealt with easily."
one core idea: to incline or draw something toward yourself by means of a sound or speech that you produce
The base verb is دَعَا / يَدْعُو / دُعَاء (to call).
Shāhid: a line of Imruʾ al-Qays ("...the people do not claim that I flee")
doubled d-r points to two root meanings: one thing issuing from another, and agitation (unsteady movement) in a thing
darra is the pouring of clouds, and clouds of abundant rain are midrār
the piercing, shining star, likened to durr and named after it for its whiteness
al-Hudhalī's verse on a pearl over which "the sweet water lingers and surges"
going ahead in order to guide.
sending a kindness.
هَدَيْتُهُ الطَّرِيقَ ("I guided him on the road") = I went ahead to direct him
الْهُدَى (right guidance) as the opposite of الضَّلَالَة (going astray)
الْهَدِيَّة (a gift) = a kindness sent to someone one loves
A verse of poetry illustrates a spear-point as a man's "guide" through the land.
resting on two root meanings: cutting, and the drawing-together of a thing
al-jubb is a well.
Abū Khirāsh, describing an eagle that lifts its prey and then lets it drop, says the prey "struck the hard ground (al-jabūb) with the place between its eyes"
the root has one core meaning: cutting (al-qaṭʿ)
arḍ juruz is land with no vegetation, as if growth had been cut off from it
Ash-Shammākh's line is cited describing a rasp in the nasal passage and nostrils.
"A hating woman will not be satisfied except with a jarzah"
one core meaning: turning/rotation, and by extension, gathering into a mass
as though the sun were entirely gathered/bundled up
He wraps/turns the one over the other and the other over the one
means to turn away and swerve off from God's dīn
المُلْتَحَد (al-multaḥad) means a refuge or shelter
A line of Ḥumayd ibn Thawr: "Enough for me of supporting the two Khubaybs, enough / the leader is not the miserly, deviating one (al-mulḥid)."
highlights.note: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: Two distinct sound roots: (1) the settling of a liquid in its resting-place, and (2) a kind of sound/outcry.
The proverb "huwa sharrābun bi-anquʿ" — "he is a drinker at [hidden] pools" — describes someone who repeats a matter over and over
naqaʿa al-ṣawt — a sound rose up, illustrated with a line of poetry about a war-cry gathering people for battle
this root carries two core meanings: (1) aiming/purposing toward something, and (2) the stone/pit of something
al-nawā meaning "the pit of a date."
analyzes ق ن ع as containing two distinct core ideas, plus a possible third
al-qāniʿ being "the one who begs," so called because he turns toward the person he's asking
iqnāʿ meaning "raising something up with no downward dip."
A supporting verse contrasts a man's well-managed wealth, which spares him need, as more honorable than begging (qunūʿ)
which the exegetes explained as "raising their heads."
a single core sense: one thing rising or mounting upon another
رَكِبَ (rakiba, "he rode/mounted")
الرِّكَاب (al-rikāb): riding-camels
الرَّكْب (al-rakb) and الْأُرْكُوب (al-urkūb): a riding party
one root whose single underlying idea is bewilderment or disorientation (ḥayra)
سُكْر (sukr) is the drunkenness produced by drink
{إِنَّمَا سُكِّرَتْ أَبْصَارُنَا} — "our eyes have merely been sukkirat", i.e. dazed
سَكَر (sakar, with two a-vowels) is simply "drink" (al-sharāb)
Shāhid: a line of Aws — "My nights are made yet longer in their length; they are neither mild (ṭalq) nor still (sākira)."
سريع = "swift": "he came swiftly"; "a swift horse," plural "swift horses" (سراع)
يسارعون / يتسارعون = "they vie and race toward the good"
Proverb: "How are the slow to overtake the swift, the short-paced the wide-striding?"
a verse by Mālik b. Zaghba al-Bāhilī on aversion arriving "so soon" while the bond of union frays
وهب (wahaba) — to give something as a gift
al-Wahhāb "the abundant in gifts."
Al-wasan and al-sinah (this author treats سِنَة as belonging to the same root) both name a light doze or drowsiness that overtakes a person
a verse by Ḥumayd ibn Thawr in which a rain-cloud "visits" a meadow the way a night-phantom visits a sleeper
highlights.note: Ḥumayd ibn Thawr, lived into Islam

highlights.text: the three letters kh-y-m form a single root meaning "to stay/reside" and "firmness, steadfastness."
al-khaymah ("tent") — well known; explicitly named for the fact that one resides (aqāma) in/at it
Supported by a line of poetry describing "a stacked frame of tent-poles" left standing [of an abandoned camp]
One sound root: elevation, rising, loftiness, and fullness/abundance.
al-farʿ — the top/highest part of a thing
illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws comparing a dull-witted man to such a swaddled calf
treats it under the core idea of "leaning / inclining,"
To incline or lean toward something: "they inclined toward peace"
janāḥ = blame/fault: "there is no janāḥ upon you" (no blame on you)
with a verse of al-Namir on hastening a she-camel "when the late afternoon declined."
two verses of al-Nābigha, one on carrion-birds trailing an army
al-milla = a trodden way, extended to "religion/way."
amalla ʿalayhi al-kitāb = to dictate a text to someone (from the sense of going over it repeatedly)
Firās al-Fazārī — a camel yearns when the shackles wore hard on her forelegs
Ibn Muqbil (the two time-spans passing over ruins, wearing them with decay)
a single core idea — swelling, rising, increasing
Q 22:5: the earth "stirs and swells (rabat)" when water descends — i.e. it increases as a growing thing does.
is, at root, "increase over the capital."
I raised him so he grew
al-Rāghib states that in the Law (sharʿ) the term was narrowed to increase of a specific kind.
To trade, to deal in merchandise.

citing Zuhayr's verse comparing his weeping eyes to the buckets of a water-drawing camel

ruwaydan) — doing an action gently, slowly.

al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza, where spears whose points are "al-qaḍāʾ"

highlights.note: Q 91:6 explained by its ordinary meaning

anything at all that you conceal or screen yourself with

Ibn Fāris explains آية القرآن (a Qurʾānic āya) as "a group of letters"

describing a youth "cut to the cut of a sword — not *mutaʾāzif*, nor flabby in chest and shoulder-flesh,"
highlights.note: the mother of Yazid b. al-Tathriyya, Umayyad; no earlier witness

highlights.text: al-azr: simply "strength" or "power."
I braced my azr [my strength/support] for him with a resolute man's firm resolve
highlights.note: al-Baʿīth, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: a seething, hissing sound

الضَّحْو (al-ḍaḥw) is the day's rising; الضُّحى (al-ḍuḥā) is slightly later
"you shall not thirst therein, nor taḍḥā" and glosses it: the sun's heat does not harm you.

ḍ-f-d-ʿ — "frog."

A verse by the poet Labīd ibn Rabīʿah describes travelers heading to springs at Lubnā or Ajā that are muḍafdiʿāt ("frog-filled")
highlights.note: Labīd ibn Rabīʿah, lived into Islam

highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core meaning for the root

A verse of Ibn Muqbil uses the same verb for tucking a weapon at one's flank-strap.
things being mixed up and tangled together
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single idea for the root

highlights.text: aḍghāth are dreams that are confused and run together.
A ḍighth is a handful of twigs or of grass

(they resemble the saying of earlier disbelievers)
Abū Isḥāq explains it as: they resembled the earlier disbelievers' saying, i.e. they said it only in imitation of them
highlights.note: exegete Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj (d. 923) on Q 9:30

highlights.text: A ḥadīth: "the people most severely punished on Judgment Day are those who yuḍāhūn God's creation"
highlights.note: a hadith, taken to cover image-makers

highlights.text: lying flat against the ground on one's side
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: ḍajaʿa, verbal noun ḍujūʿ — to lie down on one's side
highlights.note: مَضَاجِع, 3x "the beds" — places of lying down

highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single meaning for the root

Anyone who swerves from the right, intended course is ḍāll, "astray."
a fitting-together (mulāʾama) of two things.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: ḍamamtu l-shayʾa ilā l-shayʾ means "I joined one thing to another"
the root d-m-r has two distinct, sound senses
damara (verb), dumur (verbal noun): said of a horse (or anything else) growing lean, from lightness of flesh
two distinct, valid roots (with few derived words)
aḍ-ḍank (الضَّنْكُ) — narrowness, constriction.
that indicates stinginess with a thing.

A rajul ḍanīn is a stingy man.
softness or pliancy in a thing
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core idea for the root

highlights.text: ḍaraʿa al-rajul, verbal noun ḍarāʿa — for a man to become abased or humble himself.
named for its weakness, since it "neither fattens nor avails against hunger."
a line of Ibn Waʿla contrasting patience with slackness
highlights.note: Ibn Waʿla, era undated in the entry

highlights.text: a saying of the Prophet about Jaʿfar's two sons: "Why is it that I see the two of them ḍāriʿayn?"
one root meaning — "to strike a blow"
ضَرَبَ = to strike, inflict a blow on another
الضَّرْب فِي الأَرْض = striking out into the land — journeying, for trade or otherwise
Qur'an 4:101, "when you journey through the land, no blame to shorten the prayer."
highlights.note: the entry's own citation of Q 4:101

highlights.text: three root meanings (uṣūl): the opposite of benefit, the gathering together of a thing, and strength.
Al-ḍarr is the opposite of benefit (nafʿ): ḍarrahu yaḍurruhu ḍarran, "he harmed him."
Iḍṭarra, "to be driven to something," comes from ḍarūra, necessity.
Al-ḍarīr is also someone harmed by the loss of his sight or by the wasting of his body.
Poets also use the form ḍārūra, as Ibn al-Dumayna does
highlights.note: Ibn al-Dumayna, Umayyad (no earlier poet named)

highlights.text: whose one meaning is light.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's one meaning for the root

highlights.text: equivalent to ضِيَاء (ḍiyāʾ, radiance) and نُور (nūr, light).
He cites 2:17, "and when it lit up what was around him" (fa-lammā aḍāʾat mā ḥawlahu)
highlights.note: أَضَاءَ, 3x — the entry's citation of Q 2:17

highlights.text: the loss, disappearance, and perishing of a thing.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: The causative أَضَاعَ / أَضَعْتُ (aḍāʿa / aḍaʿtu) = "to cause something to be lost, to let it go to waste."
one thing inclining or leaning toward another
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's one meaning for the root

highlights.text: ضِفْتُ الرَّجُلَ = I presented myself to a man so he would take me in; أَضَفْتُهُ and ضَيَّفْتُهُ = I lodged him with me
ضَيْف serves for both singular and plural, and also takes the plurals أَضْيَاف and ضِيفَان.
Imruʾ al-Qays: "when we entered it, we propped our backs against every new striped Ḥīran cushion"
he cites a ḥadīth forbidding the ṣalāh when the sun has so inclined toward setting
highlights.note: a hadith on the time of ṣalāh

highlights.text: ضِيق (ḍīq) is the opposite of "roominess" — narrowness, straitness.
highlights.note: the root's core sense in Lisān al-ʿArab

highlights.text: ضاقَ ("became narrow"), with verbal nouns ḍīq and ḍayq
ḍayq is the narrow thing itself; ḍīq is the abstract verbal noun.
Qurʾan 11:12, "...and your breast being straitened (ḍāʾiq) by it."
al-Aʿshā: God "lifted the ḍayqa [hardship] from us"
ḍāqa is given as the plural of ḍāʾiq (Zuhayr's line "narrow of resting-ground")
one underlying sense, which he equates with al-ḍayr and al-maḍarra — "harm."
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single sense of the root

highlights.text: The verb yaḍīru is given as equivalent to yaḍurru ("to harm")
qisma ḍīzā ("a ḍīzā division/share"): a deficient apportionment, i.e. a share that shortchanges someone
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core sense of the root

highlights.text: "so your right is denied [maḍʾūz], and your nose is humbled"
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: two sound bases: (I) a specific number — "ten" — which is then extended to other things, and (II) mingling and entering-into
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's two origins for the root

highlights.text: عَشَرَة "ten" (masc.), عَشْر (fem.).
عَشِير = one who associates with you
عَشِيرَة (kin-group) is so named from members' mutual association; even a husband is his wife's عَشِير
الْمَعْشَر = any group united in one affair
(Shāhid: Zuhayr, on long companionship breeding weariness.)
Imruʾ al-Qays: "the shattered pieces — أَعْشَار — of a slain heart"
a hadith about women: "you curse much and are ungrateful to the ʿashīr [companion/husband]"
highlights.note: a hadith, used for the sense of ʿashīr

highlights.text: a single sound root meaning darkness and lack of clarity in a thing
ʿishāʾ — the first darkness of nightfall
al-ʿashiyy — the end of the day (late afternoon/evening)
Zuhayr's famous line likens the fates (al-manāyā) to the random trampling of such a night-blind she-camel
(shāhid: al-Ḥuṭayʾa, on coming to a generous man's fire)
its words do not follow analogy and cannot be reduced to one underlying meaning
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: the root has no one underlying meaning

highlights.text: عَذُبَ الْمَاءُ (ʿaḏuba, verbal noun ʿuḏūba) = the water became sweet/pleasant; the adjective is عَذْب (ʿaḏb, "sweet")
Torment / punishment (al-ʿaḏāb). The verb is عَذَّبَ (ʿaḏḏaba, "to torment")
citing Zuhayr (a beast that "when she fears the ʿaḏāb [the beating] stretches out her back and neck")
a ḥadīth, "Refrain (aʿḏibū) from the mention of women,"
the root ʿ-dh-r has many branches but no single unifying meaning — each cluster stands on its own
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: no single unifying meaning

highlights.text: a person's attempt, by speech, to set right something for which he has been blamed
Verb of apologizing: iʿtadhara ("he made excuse for his sin"); noun al-maʿdhira.
"qālū maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum" — "as an excuse before your Lord" (7:164)
ʿadhdhara (form II) = to make a show of exerting oneself while actually slacking
Shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays: she "proved hard against me and swore an unbreakable oath."
Ḥadīth: "the Jews are the foulest of creatures in ʿadhira," i.e. in their courtyard
highlights.note: a hadith, giving ʿadhira the sense "forecourt"

highlights.text: one sound root: holding on to a thing with the teeth
The primary use is biting with the teeth: ʿaḍiḍtu, aʿaḍḍu ("I bit, I bite")
Al-Aṣmaʿī's proverb, "You are like one who turns back to the one who bites"
al-Aʿshā describes choice white camels "hardened by ʿuḍḍ, by grazing the reserved pasture, and by long barrenness"
a sound root pointing to a bodily organ, and that this is then used metaphorically for strength and for a helper/supporter
Al-ʿaḍud is the upper arm (elbow to shoulder)
By metaphor, al-ʿaḍd means help/support — "ʿaḍadtu fulānan" = "I supported him."
highlights.note: عَضُد in the sense of support (Q 28:35)

highlights.text: The entry cites Qur'an 18:51, "Nor was I to take the misleaders as a supporter [ʿaḍudan],"
A weak or unhelpful person could be mocked as "the chipped ʿaḍud" (a Bedouin saying quoted here)
Al-ʿaḍad (different vowel) names a disease of the upper arm/foreleg, illustrated with a verse of al-Nābigha
A ḥadīth about Medina is quoted: "its trees are not to be cut [lā yuʿḍad]."
one core idea: intensity/hardship combined with twistedness — something that resists being straightened out or resolved
ʿAḍaltu l-marʾata / ʿaḍḍaltuhā — to unjustly bar a woman from marrying
glossing ʿaḍl here as taḥbis — "restrain/confine,"
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's gloss of ʿaḍl in Q 2:232

highlights.text: Illustrated by a verse attributed to Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ, who couldn't get his people to pay one wife's dowry
illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws describing a plain "sickened" and "constricted" by a huge host.
ʿUmar's remark that the people of Kufa had worn him out (aʿḍala bī)
a single idea runs through this root — dividing a thing into parts
"those who made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn." Al-Khalīl explains ʿiḍīn as "portion by portion" — they split the Qur'an up
"the religion of God is not something fragmented" (بِالْمُعَضَّى)
highlights.note: Ruʾba, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: "there is no taʿḍiya in an inheritance" — meaning one must not divide up an inheritance item that cannot bear division without ruining its value, giving a sword or a pearl as examples.
highlights.note: a hadith, on dividing an inheritance

highlights.text: one sound root whose single idea is BINDING one thing to another — either lengthwise or by wrapping round
Al-ʿuṣba per al-Khalīl is ten men, and nothing fewer is called that; it is so named because it is "bound," as if tied one to another
ʿUṣba and ʿiṣāba are used of people, birds and horses
al-Nābigha: bands of birds circling over armies, guided by other bands
يوم عصيب / يوم عصبصب, a hard day
Ḥassān — men are "people of ʿaṣb and manliness."
those who inherit by kalāla, without parent or child; in the fixed-share system, anyone whose share is not named is ʿaṣaba and takes what remains after the fixed shares
a single sound root whose core notion is lightness and speed
ʿaṣf — chaff and dry plant matter. The husk of straw on the grain
ʿāṣif — a violent, sweeping wind. Cited from Q 10:22, "a ʿāṣif wind came upon them,"
"sweeps away" a people, as in al-Aʿshā's line about a dense army that carries off armoured and unarmoured men alike
some commentators explain ʿaṣf as any crop whose grain has been eaten and whose straw is left
highlights.note: commentators' reading of ʿaṣf in Q 105:5

highlights.text: one sound root with a single core idea in three shades: holding back, preventing/withholding, and clinging/adhering
iʿtaṣama bi-llāh = he shielded himself [by holding to God]; istaʿṣama = he sought refuge.
aʿṣamtu fulānan = I gave someone a handhold to cling to.
al-ʿiṣma also = anything you hold fast to
Shāhid: al-Nābigha — the frightened sailor clings to the rudder-pole in dread and thunder.
three separate sound roots: (1) an age or stretch of time; (2) squeezing something until its liquid runs out; (3) clinging to something and taking hold of it for protection
ʿaṣr = time, an age (dahr). Cited from the Qur'an: "By al-ʿaṣr, man is indeed in loss" (103:1)
Imruʾ al-Qays: "Good morning to you, O worn ruin — but can one greet with good morning a man of the ages gone by?"
ʿuṣāra = what runs out of a thing you press; the same as ʿaṣīr (pressed juice)
Aws: "There is no recovery from Ḍabbāʾ while oil is still pressed."
al-muʿṣirāt = clouds that bring rain — "And We sent down from the muʿṣirāt water pouring forth" (78:14)
iʿṣār = dust rising in a circling column (whirlwind); plural aʿāṣīr
He also cites a ḥadīth in which "keep to the two ʿaṣrs" is explained as a prayer before sunrise and one before sunset
highlights.note: a hadith, on the two ʿaṣr prayers

highlights.text: "And in it they yaʿṣirūn" (12:49) was explained as "they draw produce from their lands"
its origin is resisting or holding out with one's staff
Al-ʿaṣā is a staff or stick
"So-and-so cast down his staff" means he halted and settled
A poet says: "so she cast down her staff, and her destination settled with her."
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: the root sense of al-ʿaṣā is gathering and concord
highlights.note: Abū ʿUbayd, quoted for the root sense

highlights.text: Defined as the opposite of obedience. ʿaṣā al-ʿabdu rabbahu: the servant disobeyed his Lord, going against His command.
Verbal nouns ʿaṣy, ʿiṣyān, maʿṣiya; the doer is ʿāṣin or ʿaṣiyy; ʿāṣāhu means the same
"Soft of staff" or "weak of staff" describes a gentle manager who rarely beats his animals, which is praise (Ibn al-Aʿrābī); verses of Maʿn ibn Aws and al-Rāʿī illustrate it
highlights.note: Maʿn ibn Aws, lived into Islam

highlights.text: "The staff is from the little staff" (al-Aṣmaʿī, on a son resembling his father)
"Do not lift your staff from your family", al-Kisāʾī and others say no literal staff or beating is meant: it is a figure for not neglecting their discipline
highlights.note: a hadith, read figuratively by al-Kisāʾī

highlights.text: "Were it not that we disobey God, He would not 'disobey' us": that is, He would not withhold His answer
highlights.note: a saying, glossing ʿiṣyān as withholding

highlights.text: Ibn Fāris states this root has one single sound sense: bending and curving
The two sides of a person are called al-ʿiṭfān because a person leans on them
the idiom thanā ʿiṭfahu, "he bent his side" — said of someone who turned away from you and treated you with coldness/disdain
a line of the poet Labīd using ʿāṭif in exactly this sense — "one who folds the cushion"
emptiness, vacancy — something left devoid or unattended
"ʿuṭṭilat al-dāru" — a house left empty, abandoned.
"an abandoned well" (Q22:45), and "when the ten-months-pregnant she-camels are left untended" (Q81:4)
a single sound meaning: taking, and handing or passing something over
ʿaṭāʾ (العَطاء) — a noun for the thing given
the sense of "giving" is derived from this root of reaching/handing
taʿāṭī (التعاطي) — a narrowed, negative use: taking or reaching for what one has no right to
Imruʾ al-Qays uses the verb taʿṭū of a woman reaching out with soft fingers
one sound root meaning largeness and strength
the verbal noun (maṣdar) of al-ʿaẓīm ("the great/mighty thing")
al-ʿaẓm — "bone," which he says belongs to this root
a coming-together under weight — things gathered up in a way that makes them heavy or bulky
the idiom mā ʿabaʾtu bihi shayʾan ("I gave it no ʿabʾ at all") means "I didn't care about it"
Cited verse: a poet speaks of "bearing the load off the necks of my people."
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: two sound but seemingly opposite roots: one meaning softness and lowliness, the other strength and hardness
al-ʿabd = an owned person (al-mamlūk)
common usage separates ʿibād Allāh ("servants of God") from al-ʿabīd ("owned slaves")
taʿabbada X ("he made X like a slave to himself, though X was free")
cited from Ṭarafa's line about being cast out like a tarred camel
an interpretation of Q 43:81, {…fa-anā awwalu l-ʿābidīn}, as "I am the first to be angered by / to disdain such a claim"
a saying attributed to ʿAlī, ʿabidtu fa-ṣamattu ("I was angered, so I kept silent")
anything unusually excellent or extraordinary — a person, an animal, or a piece of cloth — used to be attributed to it
highlights.note: the sense the entry gives ʿabqarī

highlights.text: ʿabqariyy denotes a kind of furnishing or carpet
the saying arose about the caliph ʿUmar: I have not seen an ʿabqarī like him
highlights.note: a report about the caliph ʿUmar

highlights.text: a single sound root whose core idea is passing through something and going on across it
عَابِر سَبِيل is one who is merely passing through
عَبَرَ الرُّؤْيَا (verbal nouns عَبْر, عِبَارَة) and عَبَّرَ (تَعْبِير) mean to explain it
اعْتِبَار and عِبْرَة (taking heed). He proposes that both come from the two facing banks of a river
al-Khalīl's definition of عِبْرَة as drawing a lesson from what has passed
Imruʾ al-Qays: "my cure is a flow of tears, if I pour it out — yet is there at an effaced camp-trace anything to lean on?"
reads Q 59:2 "So take heed, O you possessed of insight" accordingly: look at those who acted and were punished
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 59:2

highlights.text: one sound root whose core notion is aversion or repugnance toward something
al-yawm al-ʿabūs, "the scowling day," meaning a day that is harsh and repellent
the verb ʿabasa / yaʿbisu / ʿubūs — to scowl
camels were passed by that had become "ʿabasat" — crusted over in their own urine.
highlights.note: a hadith, for the concrete sense

highlights.text: one sound root with a single core meaning: mixing (al-khalṭ)
the word "al-ʿabath" came to denote an action done without evenness or soundness
glosses ʿabathan here as laʿiban ("in play/sport," i.e., without purpose).
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's gloss of ʿabathan in Q 23:115

highlights.text: Units put together, or the putting together of units; al-Rāghib says the two definitions are the same.
highlights.note: al-Raghib's definition of al-'adad, the root's base sense

highlights.text: Joining numbers one to another.
A thing that is "counted and enumerated" (maʿdūd) is few
"We have not made their number" (Q 74:31) means their count.
"I made this ready for you" means "I placed it so that you can count on it and take it as you need it."
Al-Rāghib defines it as the days after which it becomes lawful for her to marry.
highlights.note: a legal definition of a woman's 'idda

highlights.text: Some jurists instead count the day of sacrifice and the two days after it as the "counted days".
FIRST ROOT — evenness, equality, straightness
highlights.note: the first of Ibn Faris's two roots

highlights.text: SECOND ROOT — crookedness/deviation
ʿadl = one who is approved and straight in conduct; upright.
ʿadl = judging by equity, deciding evenly.
the mushrik who yaʿdilu bi-rabbihi — treating another as equal to his Lord.
highlights.note: the entry's reading of the Qur'an's ya'dilun bi-rabbihim

highlights.text: A verse of Zuhayr uses ʿadl of trusted arbiters who are "accepted, and just."
has no single underlying sense that unifies its uses
highlights.note: Ibn Faris: no one sense unites the root

highlights.text: the well-known legume — lentils — is called "ʿadas."
"When I load my gear upon ʿadas," where "ʿadas" stands for the female mule herself
one sound root whose whole family turns on a single idea: going beyond something, overstepping the limit at which one ought to stop
Going past one's proper bounds.
The ʿādī is one who assaults people wrongfully (ẓulman wa-ʿudwānan).
Derived from the same root; the one form serves singular, dual, and plural.
Cited with Qurʾān 26:77 (Abraham: "they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the Worlds")
Cited with Zuhayr, where a distraction (ʿadāʾ) kept the poet from his beloved.
felling one after the other (cited with Imruʾ al-Qays)
cited with the ḥadīth "No ʿadwā, and nothing transmits [disease] to anything."
refraining from what is foul, and the scantness of something
al-ʿiffa is refraining from what is not fitting.
Al-ʿufra names a color: dust-gray shading into red. From this, plain earth/soil itself is called al-ʿafar.
